records.name_note: Sources split slightly on the common name. NC State's dedicated page for this taxon leads with "Black-eyed Susan Vine": its page-title parenthetical reads "(Black-eyed Susan Vine, Thunbergia)", and its alphabetized Common Name(s) list shows the same two names in the same order, so "Vine" is kept. RHS's dedicated page gives the shorter "black-eyed Susan" with no "Vine" (page title "Thunbergia alata | black-eyed Susan") and lists "black-eyed clock vine, bright eyes" as other common names. NC State says it has no relation to black-eye Susans (Rudbeckia hirta), so nothing is borrowed from that record.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: NC State's page for this species carries no poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag, and RHS's dedicated profile, read and cited here, carries no toxicity entry; no admissible source names cats or dogs. The auditor, reading MoBot's dedicated page (taxonid=275277) in a browser, reports no toxicity statement there either; MoBot refuses this machine, so it is not cited.
is_edible null: no admissible source addresses eating this plant.

MoBot (plantfinder.mobot.org / www.missouribotanicalgarden.org) page for Thunbergia alata could not be loaded: TLS 'unable to get local issuer certificate' through the sandbox proxy in curl and in verify_quotes.fetch, so nothing is cited from it.

Clemson HGIC returned 403 and its only hit is a multi-species annual-vines page, so it is not used. No dedicated UF/IFAS, PSU, UMD or UGA page for this exact species was found; the PSU and UMD hits are for Rudbeckia (Black-Eyed Susan), a different plant.

water_regime null: NC State's 'medium moisture' is a soil adjective in prose and RHS's Moisture field ('Moist but well-drained or Well-drained') is not a watering statement; neither frames a watering regime. Structured moisture is mid-scale.
soil_drainage moderate rests on NC State's 'rich, medium moisture, well-drained soils' and RHS's 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained'; no source wants wet soil.
soil_base garden_bed is a classification for the in-ground annual-vine use; NC State also lists containers and hanging baskets, which would be standard potting.
soil_ph_min/max null: RHS lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' (no bounds) and NC State gives no pH.
outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists 'Full sun' and 'Partial Shade' (mapped to part_shade); RHS Position is full sun only. NC State prose says full sun with some afternoon shade.
direct_sun_hours_max null: NC State's hour ranges appear only in the site-wide light legend; species prose gives no hour figure.

Mature size uses NC State's own Dimensions block (Height 3-8 ft, Width 3-6 ft), converted to inches (36-96 in and 36-72 in). climbs is true: NC State's Climbing Method field reads Twining, its Plant Type field lists Vine, its Habit/Form field lists Climbing, and its Description says 'As a twining vine, it does best with support so plant near an arbor, trellis or fence'; RHS calls it a 'perennial twining climber, often grown as an annual, to 2.5m tall'. Under the catalog's climber rule the published height lands as the vine's reach given support, not a free-standing height. RHS differs: Max Height 1.5-2.5 metres (59.1-98.4 in), Max Spread 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in). MoBot's dedicated page (read by the auditor in a browser; MoBot refuses this machine, so it is not cited) gives the same Height 3.00 to 8.00 feet and Spread 3.00 to 6.00 feet and says 'As an annual, it will grow to 3-8’ tall in a single season.', adding that the vine 'eventually climbs to 20’ in frost free areas'; the landed range is the reach as an annual, not the frost-free perennial's. Houseplant size rule: is_houseplant is true and no admissible page gives an indoor or container figure; the published figures are under 120 in, so they stand.
NC State warns that because it reseeds easily and in frost-free areas, it can be weedy (Weedy is also in its Problems field and tags). It is a tender evergreen best grown as an annual.

is_houseplant is true only on NC State's #houseplant and #interiorscape tags; the overwinter-in-containers advice is not houseplant framing. NC State also notes indoor plants can suffer from spider mites, scale, or white flies.
Not borrowed: the clock vine Thunbergia grandiflora is a different species and no record from it or from Rudbeckia hirta is used.
No admissible source gave temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizer or watering-interval figures; those fields are null.

toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible page names cats or dogs. NC State has no poison block and no Problem for Cats/Dogs tag, and RHS's profile carries no toxicity statement (the auditor reports the same of MoBot's page, read in a browser; MoBot refuses this machine, so it is not cited).

is_edible is true for leaves and stems only, per NC State's Edibility field ('The leaves and stems can be eaten.'). No other part is addressed, no preparation instructions are given, and neither NC State nor RHS carries a toxicity or not-to-be-eaten warning.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's Light field is full sun and its description says it will not grow in shade, which outranks the '#partial shade tolerant' tag. That tag is disclosed but not mapped to part_sun or part_shade.

soil_drainage left null. NC State's Soil Drainage field is a bare Good Drainage with no moisture value, and RHS's Moisture field reads Well–drained; a bare well-drained rating is ambiguous on this scale. The auditor read MoBot's Culture text in a browser: 'Cool weather annual or short-lived perennial that is easily grown in sandy, poor to average, well-drained soils in full sun. Sharp soil drainage is essential.' That would support fast, but MoBot refuses this machine, so the quote cannot be checked against a cached page and no value may rest on it. NC State's washes, flats and hot dry poor-soil sites are habitat and tolerance, not a drainage rating.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0). The Alkaline band is open-ended, so no ceiling can be set, and the Neutral band's 6.0 bottom is not used as a floor because RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', accepting acid as well as alkaline soils. The auditor reports that MoBot gives no pH.
soil_base garden_bed is taken from the page's statement that it suits garden beds, borders and rock gardens. The same sentence also lists containers.

attracts_pollinators true rests on RHS's Eschscholzia californica profile, which carries the Plants for pollinators badge. NC State has no Attracts field; its 'Pollinator Garden' Landscape Theme entry and '#wildlife friendly' tag name no pollinator, and the auditor reports MoBot's page names none either.
water_regime left null: no watering statement. The page says only that it is drought-tolerant and suits plants of similar watering needs, which is a tolerance trait, not a watering instruction.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual and Wildflower and its USDA zone line runs 6a-10b. Its 'start the seeds indoors about 3 weeks prior to the last frost date' is seed starting, and RHS's 'Can be grown as a drought-tolerant pot plant.' is container growing, not houseplant framing. Temperature, humidity, light fc, fertilizer and chill-damage fields have no admissible-source support and are null. The USDA zone line (6a-10b) is a hardiness range and not a damage-onset temperature.

Mature size is NC State's Dimensions block (Height 1-2 ft, Width 1-2 ft; 12-24 in each). RHS's profile gives Max Height 0.1-0.5 metres and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in) and describes 'A vigorous, spreading annual to 30cm tall'; those smaller UK figures were not merged in.

records.name_note: NC State says the common name, bacopa, is somewhat confusing since there is another genus of plants called Bacopa, commonly known as water hyssop, that are primarily aquatic plants. NC State lists the former names Manulea cordata and Sutera cordata, and its phonetic spelling line reads soo-TER-ah cor-DAH-tah, matching the Sutera cordata spelling. NC State's page-title parenthetical also carries the aliases Trailing Phlox and White Phlox. No source other than NC State was used for the common name: Bacopa is the first name in NC State's page-title parenthetical and in its alphabetized Common Name(s) list, which are in the same order, and its description opens with 'Ornamental bacopa'. RHS's dedicated Chaenostoma cordatum page gives no common name and lists 'Bacopa misapplied, Sutera cordata' under Synonyms.
unknowns: Only NC State Plant Toolbox gives species-level care data for Chaenostoma cordatum among the admissible sources. RHS has a dedicated Chaenostoma cordatum page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/259091/chaenostoma-cordatum/details), but it carries no common name and no sun, soil, pH, hardiness or size fields, only Synonyms ('Bacopa misapplied, Sutera cordata'), Family Scrophulariaceae, a genus-level description and Name Status 'Correct'; RHS's other pages for this name are cultivar pages (e.g. 'Snowflake'), which were not used. MoBot Plant Finder could not be loaded from the sandbox (certificate failures), and its basic search returns no results for Sutera, Chaenostoma or bacopa. No UF/IFAS, Clemson, PSU, UMD or UGA species page was found.
toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: NC State carries no poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag for this plant, and no admissible page naming cats or dogs was found.

is_houseplant is false: NC State says 'In North Carolina, it is best grown as an annual in hanging baskets or containers or as a ground cover along borders.' and that it is winter hardy in zones 9 to 11; it never frames the plant as an indoor plant and carries no #houseplant tag.
humidity_need is high from a single prose sentence (prefers a humid environment); no percentage is given.

Light: NC State's structured Light field is Partial Shade only, while its prose says 'It thrives in bright, indirect light'. Only part_shade is included. full_sun and part_sun are not added since no other admissible source gives a sun field for this taxon (RHS's dedicated Chaenostoma cordatum page carries none). direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour range (2-6) is the site-wide legend inside the Light field, not species prose.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State's structured pH lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and the acid band is open-ended. The prose says slightly acidic to neutral without numbers. RHS's dedicated page carries no pH field to check a ceiling against.
soil_base is null: NC State says moist, well-drained loamy soil and lists container and hanging-basket use, but no source names a potting-mix type.

water_regime and the watering-interval fields are null: NC State says only 'Water containers regularly in hot weather'. Its structured Moist drainage tag is a soil adjective, not a watering statement. There is no dormant-season guidance.
Fertilizer: NC State says to feed with an all-purpose liquid fertilizer during the growing season, with no interval, dilution or months, so those fields are null.

chill_damage_f is null: NC State gives only a hardiness range (winter hardy in zones 9 to 11), which is not a damage-onset temperature. Temperature ranges are null: the page says only moderate temperatures.
is_edible and attracts_pollinators are null: NC State has no Attracts field and says nothing on eating the plant.
NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and matches the order of the page-title parenthetical. It begins with Bacopa.
Nothing is taken from this catalog's Phlox records despite the Trailing Phlox and White Phlox aliases, and no water-hyssop (Bacopa) or medicinal text is used.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page for this hybrid has the H1 'Citrus x latifolia' (ASCII x, normalised here to the multiplication sign) and a Common Name(s) list reading Lime, Limes, Persian Lime, Tahiti Lime. The list is alphabetized, and the page-title parenthetical gives the same four names in the same order. Its Description opens with the bare umbrella name: 'Lime, also known as tahiti lime or persian lime'. The record is filed under Persian Lime, the name RHS's profile for Citrus × latifolia (F/S) (Name Status Correct) leads with. RHS lists 'bearss lime, Tahiti lime' under Other common names and gives Citrus × latifolia 'Tahiti' and Citrus 'Tahiti' as synonyms. The sources split on the lead name: UF/IFAS's 'Tahiti' lime page opens its Common Names line with 'Tahiti' lime, then 'Persian' lime and 'Bearss' lime. The bare Lime is not used: it would not distinguish this plant from Key Lime (Citrus × aurantiifolia), which this catalog already lands.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's only toxicity-type content is a human-scoped contact dermatitis problem. Under 'Insects, Diseases and Other Plant Problems' the page says: 'This plant may cause contact dermatitis in some people.' Its Landscape 'Problems' field lists Contact Dermatitis, and its tags include #contact dermatitis and #edible fruits. NC State has no Poison block, no poison-part list, no symptom list, no severity rating, and no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag. Plant Type as rendered: Edible, Houseplant, Perennial, Shrub, Tree. Edibility field: 'Fruit and juice are edible.' RHS's profile for Citrus × latifolia (F/S) gives, under Potentially harmful: 'Fruit harmful to skin with sunlight/skin allergen (lemon and lime-bearing Citrus only). Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling'. This is a fruit-handling warning covering sun-activated skin harm and skin allergy, and RHS scopes it to lemon- and lime-bearing Citrus, a group that includes this lime. RHS names the fruit and a sunlight trigger where NC State says only 'This plant'. Neither source scopes any hazard to cats or dogs.
unknowns: Three admissible pages cover this lime. NC State's dedicated page, plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/citrus-x-latifolia/, is the main source. RHS's profile for Citrus × latifolia (F/S), plant 143110 (Name Status Correct), agrees on Position 'Full sun' and Moisture 'Moist but well–drained'; its 'Tahiti' record, plant 48650, has Name Status Synonym. UF/IFAS EDIS HS8/CH093, 'Growing 'Tahiti' Limes in the Home Landscape', is a dedicated page for the same lime. Its Scientific Name line drops the hybrid sign and lists C. aurantifolia, Key lime's binomial, as a synonym, so it supplies no name evidence. RHS's Cultivation paragraph is genus-wide Citrus text, identical on its Key lime profile, and is not species evidence. Guessed Clemson HGIC and MoBot URLs gave no page for this taxon.

NC State contradicts itself on shade and wet soil. The structured Resistance To Challenges field lists Heavy Shade and Wet Soil, while the prose says 'It does not tolerate shade.' and the tags say #shade intolerant and #wet soils intolerant. Neither tolerance is landed; outdoor_sun_exposure carries only full_sun, which the structured Light field and the prose both state.

toxic_to_pets is null: no admissible source names cats or dogs. NC State's only toxicity content is a contact dermatitis problem 'in some people', with no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs value or tag, and RHS's Potentially harmful field (fruit harmful to skin with sunlight, skin allergen, wear gloves when handling) names no animal.

is_edible is true for the fruit and juice: NC State's Edibility field reads 'Fruit and juice are edible.', and its Uses (Ethnobotany) field lists the juice in drinks, syrups, jams and marinades and the fruit as a garnish. No page gives an edibility statement for leaves or other parts or a preparation condition. The hazards on the pages are skin hazards, not eating hazards: NC State says 'This plant may cause contact dermatitis in some people.', and RHS's Potentially harmful field reads 'Fruit harmful to skin with sunlight/skin allergen (lemon and lime-bearing Citrus only). Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling'.

water_regime is null: the page gives only a soil adjective ('kept moist but drains well'), 'watered regularly especially during times of drought', and an overwatering/root-rot warning, with no watering-interval or dry-down statement. Soil Drainage is Good Drainage plus Moist, which is read as moderate.

soil_ph_max is null. NC State's Soil pH field lists Alkaline (>8.0), which is open-ended, and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and its tags say #alkaline soils tolerant. RHS's pH field for Citrus × latifolia (F/S) reads 'Acid or Neutral', which excludes alkaline soil and gives no number. UF/IFAS says 'Tahiti' lime trees are susceptible to iron deficiency under alkaline and high-pH soil conditions. The sources disagree on alkaline soil and none gives a numeric ceiling, so none is landed. soil_ph_min 6.0 rests on NC State's stated 'Lime prefers a pH level of 6.0 or higher'; RHS's Acid band gives no figure to set against it.

chill_damage_f is 28, the leaf-damage onset on UF/IFAS's 'Tahiti' lime page, which also gives wood damage below about 26°F (-3°C) and severe damage or death below 24°F (-4°C). NC State gives only USDA zones 9a-11b and RHS only hardiness rating H3; both are hardiness ratings, not damage onsets. The same UF/IFAS paragraph ranks this lime as hardier than 'West Indian' (Key) lime, so the figure is this lime's own, not a parent's.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: the '6 or more hours' in the Light field is the site-wide light-category legend text, not species prose, and gives no maximum.
Fertilizer is given only as 'fertilized 3 or 4 times a year', with no strength, months or day interval, so no interval is derived.

The four size fields are null under the houseplant size rule: is_houseplant is true and no admissible page gives an indoor or container figure. NC State's Dimensions block for the hybrid's own page reads 'Height: 8 ft. 0 in. - 20 ft. 0 in.' and 'Width: 8 ft. 0 in. - 20 ft. 0 in.' (96-240 in each), and its prose says the tree reaches 'a height and spread of about 20 feet in tropical/sub-tropical regions'; UF/IFAS gives 'a height and spread of about 20 feet (5 m)' and advises keeping pruned trees at 6-8 feet; RHS's profile gives Max Height 2.5-4 metres and Max Spread 1-1.5 metres (98.4-157.5 in and 39.4-59.1 in) and describes 'An evergreen tree to 3m tall', adding that 'Limes are best grown in a cool or temperate greenhouse or conservatory and moved outside during the summer months'. None of these figures is tied to indoor or container growing by its own sentence, and the outdoor stature exceeds 120 in, so all four stay null.
Humidity, indoor light (foot-candles) and temperature ranges are not stated on the page and are left null.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Rubus occidentalis page renders an alphabetized four-item Common Name(s) list (Blackberry, Blackcap, Black Raspberry, Dewberry) in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, so the list leads with Blackberry; its Description opens by calling the plant "Black raspberry". RHS's dedicated Rubus occidentalis page is titled with "black raspberry" and lists black American raspberry, blackcap, blackcap raspberry and thimbleberry as other common names. Black Raspberry is the landed name because both dedicated pages use it, NC State in its Description prose and RHS in its page title; Blackberry, the first name in NC State's list, is not used because it is already the landed common name of Rubus allegheniensis (b12) and Rubus fruticosus (b45) in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for this species carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag, and RHS's page carries no Potentially harmful row, so no toxicity or pet-safety rating is recorded. NC State's Uses (Ethnobotany) field reads: "Flavorful fruit can be eaten raw or cooked as a topping, filling, or jam. It is of variable quality, with the finest forms having a rich acid flavor. Young shoots can be eaten raw or cooked like rhubarb. They are harvested as they emerge through the soil in the spring while they are still tender, and then peeled. A tea is made from the leaves or from the bark of the root." Its Edibility field reads: "The fleshy fruits are sweet and slightly tart in flavor; they detach cleanly and easily from their receptacles. Excellent flavor." Its Plant Type field lists Edible alongside Native Plant, Perennial and Shrub, and its tags include #edible fruits. Its Appendage field lists Prickles and Thorns, and its Stem Description says "Scattered along the length of each cane are prickles that are short and curved."
unknowns: Only two admissible dedicated pages were found: NC State and RHS. RHS's page carries no size, sun, soil, watering or hardiness fields, so every cultural field rests on NC State alone. No dedicated MoBot, Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU, UMD or UGA page for this exact species was found; genus-level or multi-species raspberry pages were not used.

toxic_to_pets left null: NC State has no Poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag and no admissible source names cats or dogs. toxicity_detail therefore records only the absence of a record plus edibility conditions and the prickle/thorn trait.

is_edible true rests on NC State's Uses (Ethnobotany) field. The fruit can be eaten raw or cooked, with no condition attached. The young shoots can be eaten raw or cooked like rhubarb, harvested as they emerge through the soil in spring while still tender and then peeled. A tea is made from the leaves or from the bark of the root. Only the shoots carry harvest and peeling conditions, and neither dedicated page names an inedible or toxic part. NC State says the fruit 'is of variable quality, with the finest forms having a rich acid flavor.'

soil_drainage left null: NC State's Soil Drainage field reads Moist and Occasionally Dry with no Good Drainage token, and the prose states only a preference for moist, highly organic soil, which supports neither fast nor moisture_retentive.

water_regime left null: NC State gives no watering statement. It gives only a soil preference ('Black raspberry prefers partial sun and moist, highly organic soil.'), a Soil Drainage field of Moist and Occasionally Dry, and the siting caution 'If planted in sites that are sunny and dry, the fruit may not develop properly without adequate rain.' None of these is a watering instruction. The next sentence, 'The canes also fail to set fruit if there is too much shade.', is a fruit-set caution about shade, not water; it matters when siting the plant in part shade.

outdoor_sun_exposure uses NC State's structured Light field (Full sun, Partial Shade, mapped to full_sun and part_shade); the prose phrase 'prefers partial sun' is not added as part_sun. direct_sun_hours_max left null because the 6-hours and 2-6-hours figures are the site-wide legend text, not species prose.

Soil pH, humidity, temperature, chill damage, indoor light, fertilizer and watering intervals have no admissible-source support and are null. NC State's USDA zones 4a-8b are a hardiness range, not a damage-onset temperature.

Mature size comes from NC State's Dimensions block, 'Height: 3 ft. 0 in. - 6 ft. 0 in.' and 'Width: 4 ft. 0 in. - 8 ft. 0 in.', converted to 36-72 and 48-96 inches. The advice to cut dead stems back to 12 to 24 inches and leave them standing for stem-nesting bees is maintenance, not size. NC State's Description says 'The canes start out growing erect to about 6 feet long in the first year, but eventually arch sideways and down and can reach the ground.' That 6 feet is the length of a first-year cane, not a separate height figure. The arching canes are not described as climbing, so climbs stays null.
NC State's Common Name(s) list and title parenthetical are both alphabetized and in the same order; the first entry is Blackberry, which is not used as the common name here.

records.name_note: NC State's page title parenthetical for Helianthus tuberosus reads "(Earth Apple, Jerusalem Artichoke, Sunchoke, Sunroot)", and its Common Name(s) field lists the same four names, one per line, in the same alphabetized order, so Earth Apple comes first in both. Its description opens "Jerusalem artichoke, (also called Sunchoke, or Sunroot)". RHS's page for this species leads with the same name: it gives the subtitle Jerusalem artichoke beneath its H1 and lists earth apple and sunchoke among its Other common names. Jerusalem Artichoke is used. NC State's "is often confused with" module lists Cynara cardunculus Scolymus Group and Helianthus decapetalus; nothing was taken from the records for those plants.
unknowns: Sources checked: NC State's dedicated page (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/helianthus-tuberosus/) is the anchor for every value. RHS's dedicated profile (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/76796/helianthus-tuberosus/details) has the H1 Helianthus tuberosus, Name Status 'Correct' and the subtitle 'Jerusalem artichoke'. It gives Position 'Full sun' only, Moisture 'Moist but well–drained', pH 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' and hardiness 'H5'; H5 is a hardiness rating, not a damage onset. Its Max Height '1.5-2.5 metres' and Max Spread '0.5-1 metres' (about 59-98 in and 20-39 in) are smaller than NC State's figures, though its description calls it 'A tall, herbaceous perennial reaching 2.5m tall or more'. MoBot's dedicated Plant Finder page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=277201&isprofile=0) fails the sandboxed fetcher on its TLS certificate chain, so it is not cited; the auditor read it in a browser. It gives 'Common Name: Jerusalem artichoke', 'Sun: Full sun to part shade', 'Water: Dry to medium' and 'Zone: 3 to 9', and its 'Height: 6.00 to 10.00 feet' and 'Spread: 3.00 to 5.00 feet' match NC State's Dimensions block. Neither RHS nor MoBot has any toxicity text, any numeric pH or any indoor-growing text. The temperature, humidity, light-intensity, watering-interval, fertilizer and chill-damage fields stay null.
toxic_to_pets is null: the NC State page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag, and no admissible source read names cats or dogs. toxicity_detail is null for the same reason.

Every prose statement read limits edibility to the tubers. NC State: 'Fresh Jerusalem artichoke tubers are edible, and are similar in texture to water chestnuts with a nutty flavor. They may be boiled, mashed, roasted like potatoes, or eaten raw.' Its Edibility field: 'Root tubers are edible raw or cooked and they resemble ginger root. They contain a high amount of inulin fiber.' It also says inulin converts to fructose. MoBot (as read by the auditor in a browser, not cited): 'Tubers may be grated raw into salads, boiled and/or mashed somewhat like potatoes, roasted or added to soups.' RHS says it is cultivated for its tubers. NC State's Plant Type field lists Edible, Herbaceous Perennial and Vegetable, and its Flower Value To Gardener field lists Edible alongside Showy, but no page says the flowers, leaves, stems or seeds are eaten or how to prepare them. The seeds are described only as food for birds. is_edible=true is a statement about the tubers.

Cultivation cautions: NC State says 'Jerusalem artichoke has the potential to become a weed problem. It spreads by rhizome, and is self-seeding to form colonies. Once established in the garden it may be difficult to remove. Any tiny piece of the plant left in the soil will sprout new plants.' Its Problems field is 'Weedy' and the description says 'Appearance tends to be weedy.' It also says the plant may require some staking or protection from strong wind, and 'Heavy clay soils prone to waterlogging will reduce yields.'

water_regime=keep_moist rests on NC State's watering sentence 'Average, dry to medium moisture is required; however, this plant is best with consistent moisture.' and its advice 'Mulch to conserve moisture.' MoBot's Culture text agrees ('Best with consistent moisture, but has some tolerance for drought.'; read by the auditor in a browser, not cited). The following counterpoints are disclosed and were not used as the basis: the 'dry to medium' clause of the same NC State sentence; NC State's Soil Drainage values Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry and its Resistance To Challenges values Drought, Dry Soil and Poor Soil; and MoBot's structured 'Water: Dry to medium' and 'Tolerate: Drought, Dry Soil, Shallow-Rocky Soil'. RHS's Moisture field reads 'Moist but well–drained'.

soil_drainage is null because the dedicated pages disagree. NC State's Soil Drainage field lists Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry, which leans toward fast. Its prose says the plant 'will tolerate most soil types as long as they are well drained' and that 'Heavy clay soils prone to waterlogging will reduce yields.' RHS's Moisture field reads 'Moist but well–drained', a moderate reading, and MoBot (read by the auditor in a browser, not cited) says plants 'generally tolerate a wide variety of soils as long as drainage is good.' No source asks for sharp or sandy drainage, and none wants wet soil.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null. NC State's Soil pH field lists two values, Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0). The Alkaline band is open-ended, so it sets no ceiling, and the prose 'is happiest in slightly alkaline soils (7-7.5)' states a preference, not a limit. RHS's dedicated profile gives pH 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so it accepts acid soils as well as alkaline ones. That rules out using the 6.0 bottom of NC State's Neutral band as a floor, just as RHS's Alkaline rules out any ceiling. The auditor reports that MoBot's page gives no pH.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: the only hour figures on the page ('6 or more hours', '2-6 hours') are parts of the site-wide Light category legend, not species prose.

outdoor_sun_exposure combines NC State's structured Light field (Full sun and Partial Shade) with its unconditional prose 'Grow in full to part sun.', which maps to part_sun. The same page says 'It does not tolerate deep shade or maritime exposure.', so full_shade is excluded. MoBot agrees (read by the auditor in a browser, not cited): its structured field reads 'Sun: Full sun to part shade', and its Culture text says 'Easily grown in average, dry to medium moisture, well-drained soils in full sun to part shade.' RHS's Position field lists only 'Full sun', and its Cultivation sentence plants tubers 'in full sun'. part_sun and part_shade stay because NC State's Light field and MoBot's Sun field both include partial shade; RHS's narrower Position is disclosed here.

is_houseplant is false. NC State's Plant Type field lists Edible, Herbaceous Perennial and Vegetable, its USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field runs from 3a through 9b, its Landscape Location field is Naturalized Area, and its description says the plant is grown 'as an edible in the vegetable garden'. RHS rates it H5, and MoBot (read by the auditor in a browser, not cited) gives 'Suggested Use: Vegetable, Naturalize'. No admissible page describes indoor or houseplant culture.

Fertilizer, humidity, temperature (including chill damage and cool rest), light in foot-candles, water intervals and the dry-down target are null: NC State's page gives no figures for them, and the plant is an in-ground perennial vegetable. The page's USDA zone list 3a-9b is a hardiness range, not a damage-onset temperature.

records.name_note: Hylocereus undatus is the older name: NC State lists it, along with Cereus undatus and Selenicereus undatus subsp. luteocarpus, under "Previously known as". The two dedicated pages split on the genus: RHS still files the plant as Hylocereus undatus (F), with Name Status Correct, while NC State's page is titled Selenicereus undatus; this record follows NC State's current name. NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list also carries Night Blooming Cereus and Queen of the Night; these are not used as the common name here. Dragon Fruit is used because it leads NC State's description ("Dragon fruit or pitaya ...") and is the name RHS gives beneath its H1.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Tags block for Selenicereus undatus reads: "#non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #edible #edible fruits #drought tolerant #sweet fruit #sweet taste #cactus #creeping #showy flowers #showy fruits #tropical #container plant #vine #arbor #long lived #climber #trellis #fragrant flowers #pollinator garden #succulent #easy to grow #perennial #fast growing #spines #night blooming". So the pet scoping is non-toxic for cats, dogs and horses. The page carries no Poison block and no symptom list; its Problems field carries one value, Spines/Thorns, and no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs value. Plant Type values as rendered: Epiphyte, Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Perennial, Succulent. Handling warning: "be sure to wear protective gloves when handling this plant due to the sharp spines along the stems." Edibility (NC State): fruits are edible and sweet, eaten fresh, in jams, or in smoothies and desserts; flowers are also edible and used for brewing tea. Caveats on the page: some people may be allergic to dragon fruit, particularly if they have allergies to other fruits, and the fruit can interact with certain medications such as blood pressure or anti-hyperglycemic agents. The page gives no preparation times or conditions. RHS's dedicated Hylocereus undatus (F) page has no toxicity statement and also calls the fruits edible, so the two sources do not disagree on edibility.
unknowns: NC State Extension's dedicated Selenicereus undatus page is the anchor. RHS has a dedicated page for this species under its older name, https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/8965/hylocereus-undatus-f/details (H1 "Hylocereus undatus (F)", Name Status Correct, subtitle "dragon fruit"); RHS's slug-only URLs without the numeric plant ID return 404. UF/IFAS EDIS HS303, "Pitaya (Dragonfruit) Growing in the Florida Home Landscape" (https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/HS303), covers "Hylocereus undatus and other species and hybrids", so it is a multi-species page and no value is taken from it. Clemson HGIC (403) and the MoBot Plant Finder (blocked from the sandbox) were reported unreachable during research.
toxic_to_pets=false rests only on NC State's tags (non-toxic for cats, dogs and horses). The page has no Poison block and no symptom list.

is_edible is true for the fruit and the flowers. Cautions on the page: possible allergy (especially in people allergic to other fruits) and possible interaction with blood-pressure or anti-hyperglycemic medication. Handle the plant with gloves because of its spines. The page gives no preparation times.
chill_damage_f is null. NC State says only that the species 'is killed by frost' and gives USDA zones 10a-11b, which are survival and range statements, not a damage-onset temperature.

Day/night temperatures, humidity percentages, foot-candles and direct_sun_hours_max are null. NC State's single Light value, "Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)", carries the site-wide category legend in its parenthesis, so its hour range was not used for direct_sun_hours_max. NC State's prose gives only "bright, direct sunlight" and "warm temperatures" with no figures, and its problems paragraph warns "Too much sun can lead to sun-scorch and dehydration." RHS's dedicated Hylocereus undatus (F) page rates the plant H1A (under glass all year) and gives Position "Partial shade" and "bright indirect light" for greenhouse culture; outdoor_sun_exposure keeps NC State's full_sun because RHS's position describes greenhouse placement, not an outdoor exposure.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null. NC State's Soil pH field lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0): the Acid band is open-ended, so it gives no floor, and the Neutral band's 8.0 top is not corroborated by RHS, whose dedicated Hylocereus undatus (F) page gives pH "Acid" only. The two sources disagree on whether neutral soil suits the plant, so no ceiling is set.

soil_drainage=moderate comes from NC State's structured Soil Drainage field, which renders three values: Good Drainage, Moist and Occasionally Dry. The prose says "This plant also prefers well-drained, loam or cactus potting mix." and warns "Overwatering or too much rainfall can lead to stem and root rot." A cactus potting mix under this field is not read as fast drainage. RHS's dedicated page gives Moisture "Well–drained" and Soil Types "Sand"; a bare well-drained rating is ambiguous on this scale, so it does not override NC State's field.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target and the watering day-interval fields are null. The two dedicated pages disagree: NC State says "Water this plant when the soil is almost completely dry and provide good air circulation to prevent disease." and "Reduce watering during the winter months, but don't allow the plant to dry out completely." (a near-complete dry-down), while RHS's Hylocereus undatus (F) page says "Water freely when in growth and apply a half-strength liquid feed monthly, keep just moist in winter." (generous watering in growth, compost kept just moist in winter). Neither gives a watering interval in days.

fertilize_strength is half, on RHS's dedicated Hylocereus undatus (F) page: "Water freely when in growth and apply a half-strength liquid feed monthly, keep just moist in winter." (species text: RHS's Epiphyllum oxypetalum page prescribes a different feed). fertilize_interval_days and fertilize_active_months are null. NC State says only "Fertilize the plant only during the growing season."; RHS's "monthly" is a word cadence, not a stated number of days, and no months are named.

climbs is true: NC State's Habit/Form field lists Climbing and Creeping, its Climbing Method field lists Clinging and Scrambler, its tags include #vine and #climber, its Stem Description says the stems "can grow up to 33 feet long and climb by aerial roots", and its Description says "Due to its climbing nature, a trellis or arbor will help it grow upright and offer the plant support." RHS describes "a vigorous, branching, epiphytic cactus with a scrambling habit" and gives Habit Trailing. The four size fields are null under the houseplant size rule: is_houseplant is true and no admissible page gives an indoor or container figure. NC State's Dimensions block reads "Height: 8 ft. 0 in. - 20 ft. 0 in." (96-240 in) and "Width: 3 ft. 0 in. - 10 ft. 0 in." (36-120 in), the climbing reach of a plant whose stems run to 33 feet; RHS's Max Height and Max Spread read 2.5-4 metres each (98.4-157.5 in), in a size panel no sentence ties to indoor growing. NC State says the plant "can be grown in containers" and suggests repotting "every 2 to 3 years or when the plant outgrows its container", with no container size. The reach exceeds 120 in, so all four stay null.
attracts_pollinators is from NC State's Attracts field (Bees, Moths) and Play Value 'Attracts Pollinators'.
NC State notes that UF/IFAS has labelled dragon fruit an invasive plant and does not recommend it in Florida. That is an outdoor-planting caveat for Florida, not a houseplant issue.

humidity_need left null: NC State's dedicated page says "The dragon fruit prefers bright, direct sunlight, warm temperatures, and moderate humidity." (average), while RHS's dedicated Hylocereus undatus (F) page says "Grow in a warm greenhouse in peat-free, epiphytic cactus compost, in bright indirect light with high humidity." (high); the two admissible sources conflict, so no category is set.

Night Blooming Cereus and Queen of the Night, both in NC State's list for this species, are also among NC State's names for Epiphyllum oxypetalum, which this catalog lands as Orchid Cactus (b44); nothing is taken from that record.
